claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in refractory alloys are governed by a balance between dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery mediated by coherent nano-precipitates.
Nano-precipitates act as pinning centers that impede dislocation glide.
Nano-precipitates enhance strain hardening at elevated temperatures.
Nano-precipitates delay crack propagation at elevated temperatures.
A controlled heat or aging treatment can create a uniform coherent nano-precipitate dispersion without changing the alloy's overall composition.
The relevant testing regime is approximately 600–1000 °C under quasi-static loading.
The proposed 600–1000 °C quasi-static testing regime is similar to anticipated fusion-reactor service conditions.
Precipitate impediment of glide increases dislocation density.
An increased dislocation density raises the strain-hardening rate.
Greater strain hardening delays the onset of plastic instability.
The precipitate-mediated deformation process enhances toughness by blunting crack tips.
The interplay between dislocation pinning and limited dynamic recovery governs both high-temperature strength and ductility.
Relative to an unperturbed single-phase baseline, a precipitate-engineered alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, a precipitate-engineered alloy will have a higher high-temperature strain-hardening rate.
Relative to the baseline, a precipitate-engineered alloy will have improved high-temperature fracture toughness while retaining acceptable ductility.
The untreated baseline has lower high-temperature yield strength and toughness because it contains fewer effective dislocation-pinning sites.
The proposed mechanism applies to refractory multi-principal-element and high-entropy alloys in fusion-relevant temperature and strain-rate regimes.
The mechanism becomes less effective if precipitates coarsen or lose interfacial coherency.
Long-term fusion irradiation may alter precipitate stability.

Failure of the precipitate-rich samples to improve yield strength, strain hardening, or fracture toughness relative to the matched baseline, or observation of adverse ductility, would falsify the hypothesis.
